PullRequest.Title: Render Blobby jump game with Babylon Lite (WebGPU)
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

Blobby's jump-game playfield is now rendered with [Babylon Lite](https://github.com/BabylonJS/Babylon-Lite) on WebGPU. The game model, input, camera, scoring, accessibility, reduced-motion behavior, pet animation and lifecycle are unchanged.

- All visible platforms and walls are batched into **one instanced draw and one buffer upload per changed frame**; unchanged frames do no GPU work.
- Platform count no longer adds DOM nodes, style recalculation, layout or paint.
- The renderer is lazily loaded only when the game starts, and falls back automatically to the existing DOM renderer when WebGPU or the GPU device is unavailable or lost.

## Performance

Measured with the production renderer modules inside the VS Code web workbench (Chromium, medians of three runs).

**Realistic long session** (1,000 retained platforms, 10 visible):

| | DOM | Babylon Lite (WebGPU) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Main-thread busy / frame | 0.767 ms | **0.402 ms** (~48% less) |
| Renderer + GPU process CPU / frame | 1.671 ms | **1.232 ms** (~26% less) |

**Stress test** (1,000 platforms visible):

| | DOM | Babylon Lite (WebGPU) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Main-thread busy / frame | 5.58 ms | **0.70 ms** |
| GPU process CPU / frame | 1.63 ms | **0.63 ms** |
| Style + layout / frame | 2.42 ms | **0.01 ms** |
| Paint / frame | 4.16 ms | **0.08 ms** |

**Visual parity:** ~0.1% pixel difference against the DOM renderer, limited to subpixel edge antialiasing.

## Packaging

- One checked-in, minified ESM bundle at `src/vs/base/browser/babylonLite/lite-webgpu.js` (~23 KB raw / ~9.5 KB gzip), vendored the same way as `marked` and `dompurify`, with `.d.ts`, license and `cgmanifest.json`.
- Reproducible with `pnpm run bundle-babylon-lite`, which tree-shakes only the APIs the renderer uses from the pinned `@babylonjs/lite` dev dependency.
- No new runtime npm dependency is shipped in the desktop or web products.

## How to test

1. Open the chat pet and start the Blobby jump game.
2. Play: platforms, walls, crumbling platforms and camera scrolling should look and behave as before.
3. Optionally launch with `--disable-gpu` (or in an environment without WebGPU) to confirm the game falls back to the DOM renderer.
4. Unit tests: `./scripts/test.sh --run src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/test/browser/widget/chatPetWidget.test.ts`

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The default high-contrast color definitions enable this branch, and the strip count and per-sprite allocations follow directly from the code. The new perimeter test also confirms 356 border sprites for just one platform and one 16-pixel-wide wall. Runtime duration and GC frequency have not been measured.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Short-lived sprite objects/arrays, border tessellation CPU work, and instance-buffer upload bytes
Findings.PerformanceScaling: A six-pixel-high platform emits 48 strips per half-cap plus two straight edges: 98 border instances, before its fill. Ten visible platforms therefore add about 980 border instances and about 3,920 object/array allocations per changed frame. Each instance occupies 52 uploaded bytes. Calls remain batched into one instance upload and one draw, not one GPU call per strip; unchanged-hash frames skip this work.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Substantially increased short-lived allocation, CPU reconstruction, and GPU-upload volume during high-contrast gameplay, producing avoidable GC/frame-time pressure.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Each visible platform or wall was a reused DOM element with a CSS border. Animation updated its position; JavaScript did not retessellate the rounded border or allocate per-strip sprite data.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: When contrastBorder is defined, every changed frame reconstructs the rounded perimeters in JavaScript and copies all resulting strip instances into the GPU upload.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The new 0.125-pixel strip loop at lines 141-154 expands each rounded border into many sprites. The new renderer clears and reconstructs the whole layer at lines 157-168 and allocates an object plus position, size, and color arrays for each emitted sprite.
Findings.Title: Avoid rebuilding subpixel-strip borders on every changed frame
Findings.Impact: With either built-in high-contrast theme, jumping or animating a visible moving platform causes this work at frame rate even for a normal handful of visible platforms. Hundreds to roughly a thousand border instances replace a handful of CSS-bordered elements.
Findings.Evidence: contrastBorder has non-null hcDark/hcLight defaults in platform/theme/common/colors/baseColors.ts:41-43 and is passed into renderer colors by ChatPetJumpGame.updateRenderer. renderChatPetJumpGameLiteShapes invokes addCapsuleBorder for every visible platform and wall. A platform's fixed height is six pixels, so each cap's loop executes 6/0.125=48 times. The callback in chatPetJumpGameWebGpuRenderer.ts:159-165 constructs four objects/arrays per instance. lite-webgpu.js creates 13-float instances and uploadSpriteInstances writes the entire rebuilt dirty range. The added high-contrast perimeter test explicitly expects 356 border sprites for its two objects.
Findings.Recommendation: Render rounded border caps with a constant-size atlas representation prepared outside the frame loop, or retain the DOM renderer for border themes until a bounded-cost GPU border representation is available.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The frame loop, moving-platform updates, visible-extents calculation, and backing-canvas width/height assignments are all traced. Reallocation frequency depends on whether a moving platform defines an unclipped horizontal extremum; exact GPU cost is not measured.
Findings.PerformanceResource: WebGPU presentation textures/drawing buffers and compositor surface updates
Findings.PerformanceScaling: One backing-buffer resize per changed frame whose rounded visible width changes, potentially at animation-frame frequency while an outermost moving platform travels. The affected buffer covers the cropped width times the full playfield height, scaled by devicePixelRatio squared; this is not a per-platform GPU call.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Repeated presentation-buffer invalidation/reallocation and surface-size churn during normal animation, adding GPU/compositor work and frame-time pressure.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The DOM renderer reused visible platform elements and updated their positions. Moving a platform did not resize or replace a WebGPU drawing buffer.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Horizontal platform motion now changes the cropped canvas dimensions whenever a moving extreme crosses an integer pixel, even though the playfield itself has not resized.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: New line 155 derives the canvas width from the current visible platform/wall extrema on each changed frame. updateCanvasBounds then invokes setEngineSize at line 188; the newly vendored setSurfaceSize writes canvas.width and canvas.height whenever that width changes.
Findings.Title: Keep the drawing-buffer size stable while platforms move
Findings.Impact: During ordinary play, a visible moving platform can define the leftmost or rightmost extent. Its motion then repeatedly reallocates the full-height drawing buffer rather than merely updating sprite positions; high-DPI and tall playfields amplify the cost.
Findings.Evidence: ChatPetJumpGame.scheduleFrame renders on each animation frame. ChatPetJumpGameModel.step updates moving platform.left sinusoidally. getChatPetJumpGameLiteRenderInfo computes left/right directly from those positions (chatPetJumpGameLiteShapes.ts:111-112). render uses floor/ceil of those extents at lines 154-155. updateCanvasBounds calls setEngineSize, whose setSurfaceSize implementation (lite-webgpu.js:151-160) assigns both canvas.width and canvas.height on any size difference. The following renderFrame obtains the presentation texture at the new size. No size buckets or hysteresis bound these changes.
Findings.Recommendation: Keep a stable playfield-sized backing buffer and update sprite positions only, or use a padded/bucketed crop whose allocation does not track each pixel of platform movement.

Scenarios.Scenario: Workbench startup without starting the jump game
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Normal workbench/widget construction does not await or initialize the new WebGPU renderer. The dynamic renderer import is reached only from the game constructor.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Zero GPU engines and zero lazy renderer/runtime loads until an explicit game start.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: No GPU initialization or new renderer frame loop before the game starts.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The WebGPU module cache is not populated during ordinary workbench startup. Production build entries keep renderer and runtime separately loadable.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: traced runtime imports and the explicit production entry-point handling.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: No startup timing measurements; the added DOM-renderer abstraction is small and does not establish a startup regression.

Scenarios.Scenario: Start a game on a supported device, an unavailable device, or after a previous game
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The existing DOM renderer lays out, renders, and starts gameplay immediately. Lazy module loading and adapter/device acquisition occur asynchronously; only promotion to WebGPU awaits them.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dynamically load renderer and Babylon Lite runtime modules.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two production lazy entry bundles on a successful cold start; development modules can load their transitive shape/helper modules. Successful warm imports reuse the module cache.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No WebGPU modules were loaded; the game used its already-loaded DOM rendering code.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the initial gameplay critical path because DOM rendering continues during loading.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Acquire GPU adapter/device, configure canvas, upload the small shape atlas, and create shader/pipeline resources.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One adapter/device request sequence and one two-frame atlas per successful game initialization; shader/pipeline caching is per device.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No explicit WebGPU initialization; visible platforms were DOM elements.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required for WebGPU promotion, not for starting gameplay.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One initialization attempt per game instance. In production, the cold path loads one renderer bundle and one runtime bundle, not one module/device per platform.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Renderer import precedes runtime import, which precedes adapter/device acquisition. Simultaneous instances can share module loading but not engine creation; there is no platform-driven initialization fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Browser ESM caching reuses successful imports. loadLiteWebGpu additionally shares a promise keyed by runtime URI and removes rejected promises. Engines/devices are intentionally created per game rather than cached across games. Missing navigator.gpu rejects before loading the runtime.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: loading order, cache ownership, DOM-first behavior, and initialization are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Cold module/driver latency and hardware behavior are unmeasured. No evidence that this bounded asynchronous initialization blocks an important scenario.
Scenarios.Verdict: No independent finding for lazy initialization or module-cache lifecycle.

Scenarios.Scenario: Ordinary gameplay with moving platforms and camera scrolling
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each scheduled animation callback advances the existing model, renders the playfield, and updates the pet/gauge before the frame can be presented.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Upload changed sprite instances, optionally update the small uniform buffer, and submit one rendered frame.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One instance-buffer upload for a nonempty rebuilt layer and one queue submission per changed frame; zero on hash-equal frames. Uniform upload occurs only when its values change.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: One reused DOM element per visible platform/wall, with style updates during each render and browser-managed layout/paint/compositing.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Synchronous command preparation is on the animation callback; GPU execution/presentation follows asynchronously.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Change canvas backing dimensions to the current rounded horizontal visible extent.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one resize from the render path per changed frame, but potentially frame-rate resizing when a moving platform defines an unclipped horizontal extremum. Buffer pixel area scales with cropped width, full height, and DPR squared.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Moving platform elements changed position without resizing any WebGPU presentation buffer.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Invalidates presentation backing storage immediately before rendering and introduces surface-size churn into the frame path.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: N retained platforms and walls are scanned for visibility/hash; changed frames scan them again to generate geometry. Only V visible objects emit instances. A normal viewport contains a handful to roughly ten platforms, even if a long session retains many more.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One synchronous render path per game animation frame. Visible sprites are grouped into one layer and one instanced draw; there is no per-platform queue submission.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Equal visible-state hashes skip geometry rebuilding and all WebGPU submission. Shader pipelines and same-count render bundles are reused. Instance arrays retain capacity. The current visible horizontal crop, however, has no padding/bucketing and can change with each pixel of outermost-platform movement.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: frame scheduling, model motion, crop calculation, canvas dimension writes, upload grouping, and hash suppression are traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The frequency with which a moving platform defines an extremum and the driver-specific resize duration are unmeasured. This affects severity, not the established mechanism.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reported repeated drawing-buffer resizing. No separate finding for the extra visibility scan or the intended batched GPU rendering.

Scenarios.Scenario: Play with either built-in high-contrast theme or a configured contrast border
Scenarios.CriticalPath: On every changed frame, all visible geometry, including borders, is reconstructed synchronously before the instance upload and presentation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Copy and upload all generated border-strip instances.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One grouped instance upload per changed frame, with 52 bytes per generated strip instance; not one upload per strip.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Reused DOM elements supplied their rounded borders through CSS; JavaScript did not generate hundreds of strip descriptors per frame.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: JavaScript tessellation, object allocation, and buffer population precede submission; allocation increases GC pressure during animation.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Each six-pixel-high platform adds 98 border instances. Ten visible platforms add approximately 980 border instances, 3,920 temporary objects/arrays, and about 51 KB of instance data per changed frame, before fills or walls. Wall border counts scale with the smaller wall dimension.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Border construction is serialized on the UI thread. All strips still share one layer upload and one draw, so this is allocation/geometry amplification rather than per-strip GPU boundary fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Theme colors are cached until a theme event, but border tessellation and sprite descriptor allocations are not cached. Hash-equal frames skip the work; camera movement or a visible moving platform invalidates the hash. Existing typed-array capacity prevents repeated capacity growth, not descriptor allocation or full dirty-range upload.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: built-in theme defaults reach the branch, exact loop counts and allocations are explicit, and the added perimeter test confirms 356 border sprites for two objects.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: No measured frame times or GC pauses. Normal visible counts and theme-specific reachability are sufficient to establish the amplification; exact user impact varies by hardware and frame rate.

Scenarios.Scenario: Resize the chat host, change themes, or pause through accessibility help
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Host layout invokes game layout synchronously. Theme changes synchronously recolor and rerender the last state. Pausing cancels the game animation callback and renders once; resuming schedules it again.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resize the drawing buffer and/or upload and submit a refreshed frame.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Layout can resize to full width and then to cropped width in the same layout/render pair; theme changes submit one refreshed frame, subject to nonempty layer upload behavior.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Layout and theme changes updated DOM-based geometry/CSS without explicit drawing-buffer resizes or WebGPU uploads.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: On the layout/theme handler critical path; no repeated work while paused absent another event.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One layout/render per host notification or theme event; visible geometry count and canvas pixel area control the rendering cost. Paused gameplay does not continue its frame loop.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous UI event handling; no additional timer/render loop is created by the Babylon engine because the integration invokes renderFrame manually.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Layout and theme changes invalidate the render hash. Layout first expands the canvas to the full playfield and the following render can shrink it to the crop even when the previous crop would fit. Theme colors are refreshed only on theme changes.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: host callers, pause/resume ownership, hash invalidation, and manual frame submission are traced.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Host notification rates and the duration of synchronous graphics calls are unmeasured.
Scenarios.Verdict: Layout crop churn shares the reported buffer-sizing root cause. No independent pause/theme scheduling regression.

Scenarios.Scenario: Exit, fall, retry, dispose during initialization, or fall back after GPU failure
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Exit cancels game scheduling and either removes effects immediately or transfers renderer ownership to a bounded 160 ms fade. Failure installs the DOM renderer and disposes the active GPU renderer. A factory resolving after game disposal is disposed instead of installed.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Destroy GPU buffers, atlas texture, and device; unconfigure the canvas.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One cleanup sequence per created renderer, either immediately, after the fade, or when stale initialization resolves.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Cleanup removed DOM platform elements and cleared maps; no explicit GPU device resources existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cleanup runs during disposal/fade completion; pending initialization does not block exit.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One renderer/device per active game, plus a bounded fading renderer. Retry retains the existing game model as before. Pending initializations can finish after exit but do not remain installed.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Fade disposal is event-driven and also owned by the widget disposable. Initialization is asynchronous and checked for staleness after resolution; the code does not globally limit initialization across separate game instances, but no realistic unbounded burst was established.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Successful module imports survive repeated starts; GPU resources, theme listeners, and device callbacks are disposed per renderer. There is no automatic same-game retry loop after failure.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for established normal, stale-resolution, fade, and fallback ownership. No additional high-confidence persistent resource leak was established.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Driver disposal cost and prevalence of overlapping pending starts are unknown; neither establishes another actionable regression here.
Scenarios.Verdict: No independent lifecycle or fallback finding.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance-review pass across the complete 20-file inventory and diff pages. Submitted two introduced performance findings: animation-driven drawing-buffer resizing and high-contrast border tessellation/allocation. Traced lazy loading, production bundling, visibility/hash behavior, grouped GPU uploads, theme/layout events, pause/resume, fallback, fade ownership, and stale asynchronous completion. Review was static; no benchmark claims were independently reproduced. The rendering rewrite is an optimization, but a separate historical regression fix with sufficiently concrete provenance was not established.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
